title: The Una's Green Water: Cabins, Travertine and Krajina Forest

bestPeriod.avoid: December–March — riverside cabins close or run cold, forest tracks to Klekovača are snowbound, and the Una runs high and brown

accommodation.note: Riverside wooden cabins €50–€90 per unit; NP camping 20 KM (€10) pp/night

food.note: Mains 12–22 KM (€6–€11); a whole grilled trout with sides under €15

transport.note: Rental car from Zagreb €40–€60/day, fuel, green card, cross-border fee

activities.note: NP zone tickets 4–12 KM, rafting €45–€60, NP guide 100 KM/day, fishing permit 50–60 KM

profile.difficultyNote: 2/5 — riverside walking, one 900 m forest ascent, and a rafting day; nothing technical

gatewayAirport: ZAG Zagreb, 2 h 30 to Bihać via the Maljevac crossing; ZAD Zadar 2 h 45; SJJ Sarajevo 4 h 30
summary: The Una is a limestone river that builds its own bed: dissolved calcium precipitates out as travertine, forming stepped barriers, terraces and curtains that shift over decades, so the waterfalls here are alive rather than eroded. Una National Park, declared in 2008, protects 198 km² of that river plus the Unac tributary and the forest above. This week is deliberately low-mileage — a rafting day from Štrbački buk, a slow day of village bread and travertine at Martin Brod, a forest day toward Klekovača's old-growth beech and spruce, and evenings on a wooden deck with the water going past at walking pace. It suits people who want genuine quiet, low prices and a country that still surprises Western visitors, and who will take the landmine briefing seriously enough to stay on marked ground.

itinerary.title: Cross the border, land on the river at Bihać
itinerary.morning: Drive from Zagreb to the Maljevac or Ličko Petrovo Selo crossing — passports out, green card in the glovebox — and into Una-Sana canton. Change money and buy a local SIM in Bihać.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk Bihać's riverside: the Captain's Tower, the Fethija mosque (a Gothic church converted in the 16th century, unmistakable from its buttresses), and the Japodski otoci, a chain of wooded river islands linked by footbridges that the town uses as its swimming and picnic ground.
itinerary.evening: Grilled Una trout and a Bosnian coffee at a riverside restaurant on the Kostela cascade below town, with the falls audible over dinner.
itinerary.dayStats: 240 km / 2 h 30 plus border / BAM pegged at 1.95583 to €1 / local SIM roughly 10–20 KM / hospital in Bihać, the only one for 100 km

itinerary.title: Štrbački buk and the upper river
itinerary.morning: Drive to Orašac and take the forest spur to Štrbački buk, the Una's signature fall — a 24 m travertine drop into a green pool, viewed from wooden platforms that put you close enough to be soaked in spray. Buy the zone ticket at the entrance gate.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the riverside path downstream and swim in one of the flat reaches; the water sits around 12–14°C even in August, so this is a plunge, not a lounge. Cross into the Lohovo zone on the way back for the quieter Troslap and Dvoslap cascades.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Kulen Vakuf below the Ostrovica fortress, a 14th-century hilltop ruin above a village of 300 people.
itinerary.dayStats: NP zone ticket 12 KM adult (≈€6.10), 8 KM child, 4 KM senior / Lohovo entrance 4 KM / Štrbački buk 24 m / 12 km gravel spur from Orašac / water 12–14°C
itinerary.sleep: Riverside cabin or pension, Kulen Vakuf

itinerary.title: Rafting the Štrbački buk section
itinerary.morning: Raft the classic run from below Štrbački buk down to Lohovo — grade II–III at normal levels, with a few genuine drops over travertine steps and long green flat stretches between. Operators supply wetsuit, helmet and shuttle; the park charges a separate small water-use fee of 15 KM for this section.
itinerary.afternoon: Dry out at the take-out, eat the standard rafting lunch of grilled meat and bread, then do nothing for three hours. This is not a filler — the river week only works if you let some days empty out.
itinerary.evening: Back in Kulen Vakuf, walk up to the Ostrovica ruins for sunset over the Una's confluence with the Krušnica.
itinerary.dayStats: 15 km river / grade II–III / operator price typically €45–€60 pp incl. equipment and shuttle / NP rafting fee 15 KM Štrbački buk–Lohovo / minimum age usually 12

itinerary.title: Martin Brod, Milančev buk and a slow village day
itinerary.morning: Drive south to Martin Brod, where the Unac joins the Una and the river disintegrates into a fan of travertine steps — Milančev buk and the Veliki and Mali buk, a hundred small falls rather than one big one. Buy the separate zone ticket.
itinerary.afternoon: Visit the 15th-century Rmanj Monastery at the confluence, then walk the village lanes past the old mills. Eat lunch where the sign is handwritten. In late September the road here smells of plum rakija being distilled in every second yard.
itinerary.evening: Nothing planned. Read on a deck. If you are here in late July, the Una Regatta — a mass descent of the river that has run since the 1990s and draws thousands of boats — turns this stretch into a festival and you should either join it or avoid the week entirely.
itinerary.dayStats: Martin Brod / Milančev buk zone ticket 5 KM adult, 3.50 KM child / 45 km from Kulen Vakuf / family package 20 KM in April–May and October–November
itinerary.sleep: Village house or cabin, Martin Brod

itinerary.title: Forest day toward Osječenica and Klekovača
itinerary.morning: With a park guide or a local driver, take the forest roads east toward Osječenica and the flanks of Klekovača (1,962 m), where some of the last old-growth beech and spruce in Bosnia stands in the Lom reserve. This is the one day that genuinely needs a 4x4 and genuinely needs someone who knows which side tracks are cleared ground.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk 8–10 km through the forest, looking for bear sign on the beech and listening for black woodpecker. Stay on the track. Mushroom season here is late September–early November and the ceps are extraordinary, within personal-use quantities and outside the park's strict zones.
itinerary.evening: Return to the valley for lamb slow-cooked under a sač (an iron bell buried in embers) — order it in the morning, it takes four hours.
itinerary.dayStats: 40–50 km of forest road / Klekovača 1,962 m / guide 100 KM (≈€51) up to 8 h / zero mobile signal for 5 h / mine-marking signs mean stop, no exceptions
itinerary.sleep: Cabin, Martin Brod or Kulen Vakuf

itinerary.title: Krušnica source, Ostrožac castle and the lower valley
itinerary.morning: Drive north to Bosanska Krupa and paddle or walk the Krušnica, a 5 km spring-fed tributary so clear it looks like the boats are floating on air. Canoe hire is cheap and the current is gentle.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue to Ostrožac, a fortress above the Una begun by the Habsburgs on a medieval base, half-ruined, half-restored, and virtually unvisited on a weekday.
itinerary.evening: Back to Bihać. Eat ćevapi in the old town, then coffee by the water while the swifts work the river.
itinerary.dayStats: 5 km Krušnica / canoe hire roughly 30–50 KM / Ostrožac 25 km from Bihać / river temperature 9–11°C at the Krušnica source

itinerary.title: Last morning on the water and out
itinerary.morning: Walk the Japodski otoci once more at 07:00, when the mist is still on the river and the town is empty, or fish a morning beat with a park permit — the Una's grayling and brown trout are the reason people fly here with rod tubes.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive north to the border and Zagreb, allowing an hour of contingency for the crossing on a summer weekend.
itinerary.evening: Zagreb, or straight to the airport.
itinerary.dayStats: Fishing permit 50–60 KM/day, 120–140 KM for three days / 240 km to ZAG / border queues of 1–2 h on July and August weekends

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Kostelski Buk
accommodationStrategy.style: riverside hotel on a travertine cascade
accommodationStrategy.description: Ten kilometres from Bihać and built directly over a working waterfall, so the sound is constant and the terrace is the point. Secure parking, a proper restaurant, reliable hot water and Wi-Fi that works — the right first and last night when everything else on this trip is deliberately basic. Roughly €70–€110 a double.

accommodationStrategy.name: Camp Lučica
accommodationStrategy.style: national park campsite and simple cabins
accommodationStrategy.description: Park-run riverside pitches and huts at 20 KM (about €10) per person per day, with the river a few metres away and the park's own staff on site. Basic sanitation, no restaurant, wood available. The cheapest legitimate way to sleep inside the park boundary and the best for early-morning otter watching.

accommodationStrategy.name: Rafting-operator wooden bungalows
accommodationStrategy.description: The rafting clubs on the Una's Bihać stretch run clusters of timber cabins with shared fire pits, outdoor kitchens and a boat trailer permanently parked outside. Rough, friendly, €50–€90 a cabin, and they will bundle the rafting day and the shuttle with the room. Book by phone or Facebook message, not through booking platforms.

logistics.connectivity: Bosnia is outside the EU and outside EU roaming. Reduced Western Balkans roaming caps exist under a 2023 EU declaration, but rates are still not domestic — buy a BH Telecom or m:tel prepaid SIM in Bihać. No signal at all on the forest roads or in the Unac canyon; download offline maps.
logistics.emergency: 112 works; 122 police, 124 ambulance. Mountain rescue in Una-Sana canton is volunteer-based (GSS) and slow to reach the Klekovača forest roads — coordinates and a working local SIM matter more than anything in your first-aid kit. Nearest full hospital: Kantonalna bolnica "Dr. Irfan Ljubijankić", Bihać. EHIC/GHIC does **not** cover Bosnia; carry travel insurance that explicitly names rafting and hiking, and be ready to pay cash and reclaim.
logistics.weather: The Una valley is humid and thunderstorm-prone from late May, with storms building over Osječenica in mid-afternoon. River level is the volatile variable: after two days of rain the rafting grade jumps and operators cancel. Autumn brings dense valley fog that does not lift until 10:00 and makes the gravel spur to Štrbački buk genuinely dangerous.
logistics.bookingWindows: Rafting on Una Regatta weekend in late July is booked out months ahead and the whole valley is full; either commit early or move your dates. Cabins otherwise need two to four weeks in July–August, and almost nothing in September. Park guides should be requested at least three days out through the NP office in Bihać.
logistics.money: The convertible mark (BAM/KM) is pegged to the euro at 1.95583, so 10 KM ≈ €5.11. Euros are accepted informally at some tourist businesses at a poor rate — change money properly. Cards work in Bihać hotels and supermarkets and nowhere else that matters: village shops, park gates, mills, fishing permits and most cabins are cash. Draw 300–400 KM on arrival. Tipping is rounding up.
logistics.transportRules: Bosnia has no motorway vignette; the short A1 sections are tolled at barriers. You need a green card for the rental — confirm with the hire desk in Zagreb before you leave and expect a cross-border fee of €30–€60. Headlights on during the day are compulsory. Winter equipment rules run 1 November–15 April. Fuel is cheaper than in Croatia; fill up before returning.
logistics.permits: Una NP charges by zone — 12 KM for the Štrbački buk–Lohovo zone, 4 KM for the Lohovo entrance, 5 KM for Martin Brod/Milančev buk, free under 7, with April–May and October–November family packages at 20 KM. Rafting sections carry small additional fees (15 KM Štrbački buk–Lohovo, 8 KM Martin Brod–Kulen Vakuf). Fishing permits are 50–60 KM per day. Camping outside designated sites is prohibited in the park. Drones need permission from the park and are restricted near the border zone with Croatia, which the river partly forms.
logistics.health: Tap water is potable in Bihać and Kulen Vakuf; treat spring and well water at cabins. Ticks are abundant in the Krajina forest April–October and TBE is present in the region — check nightly. Nose-horned viper occurs on sunny limestone. And above all: the landmine issue is real, historic front-line ground runs through this landscape, and the rule is absolute — stay on paths, roads and grazed land.

proTips: Go to Štrbački buk before 09:00 or after 17:00. Between 11:00 and 15:00 in July it fills with day-trippers bussed from the Croatian coast, and the platforms are only so wide.
Buy the April–May or October–November family package at 20 KM if there are three or more of you — it undercuts individual zone tickets across two entrances.
Ask your cabin host to order sač lamb or veal in the morning for that evening. It is the single best meal in this valley and it cannot be done on demand.

The park's own guide at 100 KM for a full day is the cheapest serious wildlife guiding in Europe and the only way to read the Klekovača forest roads correctly. Book it for the day you would otherwise waste.
Carry small notes. A 100 KM note at a village mill or a park gate will produce a genuinely awkward five minutes.
Time your visit around the Una Regatta in late July deliberately — either in it, for one of the great river parties of the Balkans, or a fortnight either side, for an empty river.
The Krušnica is more beautiful than the Una at its own confluence and almost nobody outside Bosanska Krupa paddles it. Two hours, gentle, and the clearest water of the week.
Photograph the travertine at Martin Brod in the hour after sunrise, when mist sits in the steps and the whole fan glows. By 10:00 the light is flat and the picture is gone.
Fill the tank in Bihać or Kulen Vakuf before any forest day. There is no fuel between Martin Brod and Drvar, and the tracks drink more than you expect.

raw.Remote access — which tracks need what: The asphalt from Bihać to Kulen Vakuf (M14.1, roughly 40 km) is fine in any car, if slow and narrow. The 12 km spur from Orašac to the Štrbački buk viewing platforms is a graded gravel forest road: passable in a standard car dry, but rutted and slick after rain, and locals will tell you a high-clearance vehicle is the honest answer in October. The forest roads climbing toward Osječenica and Klekovača from Drvar and Martin Brod are genuine 4x4 ground — 18–25 km of loose limestone, logging traffic, no barriers and no phone signal. After snow they are impassable until May.
raw.Last-mile walk-ins and transfers: Štrbački buk is a 400 m walk and 150 wooden steps down from the upper car park. Martin Brod's Milančev buk is reached on foot through the village in under 15 minutes. The park office in Bihać (JP NP Una) arranges guides at 100 KM (about €51) for up to eight hours, and rafting operators shuttle you and your car between put-in and take-out as part of the price — the only practical way to do the upper river.
raw.Wilderness isolation — Level 3 of 5 at M: 5 min to paved road but 45 min to a supermarket in Bihać, nearest fuel at Kulen Vakuf or Bosanski Petrovac, nearest pharmacy Bihać, nearest hospital Kantonalna bolnica "Dr. Irfan Ljubijankić" in Bihać (55–70 min from Martin Brod). Klekovača forest days push this to Level 4: two hours to a hospital, no neighbours within 8 km, no signal.
raw.Off-grid reality: Riverside cabins are mostly grid-connected but with thin supply — expect a wood-burning stove as the real heat source, firewood stacked outside and included, an electric shower that dislikes being run twice at once, and septic wastewater that will not take anything but paper. Water is generally municipal and drinkable in Bihać and Kulen Vakuf, but cabin supply drawn from springs or wells should be treated. Carry a head torch, a power bank, a filter bottle, insect repellent and any specific food you need: village shops sell bread, ajvar, cheese, coffee and beer, and nothing else.
raw.Phone signal: BH Telecom and m:tel cover the valley floor and both towns; nothing in the Klekovača forest or the Unac canyon. Bosnia is **not** in the EU roaming zone — EU SIMs roam at non-domestic rates even with the reduced Western Balkans caps agreed in 2023, so buy a BH Telecom or m:tel prepaid SIM in Bihać for a few euros and stop worrying.
raw.Named cabins and character: Hotel Kostelski Buk at Kostela sits directly on a travertine cascade 10 km from Bihać, with the noise of the falls in every room. Camp Lučica, run by the national park, offers riverside pitches and simple cabins at 20 KM per person per day. Rafting operators around Golubić and Ćelije run clusters of wooden bungalows with shared fire pits — rustic, cheap, and loud on regatta weekends.
raw.Foraging rules: Bosnia's mushroom culture is strong and largely informal — vrganj (cep), lisičarka (chanterelle) and smrčak (morel) are the prizes, and the season peaks late September to early November. Federation forestry rules require permission from the cantonal forestry authority for commercial collection; personal-use picking is tolerated without paperwork, but collecting inside Una NP's protected zones needs park permission and is prohibited in the strict-protection core. There is no reliable public mycological inspection point in Una-Sana canton — assume you are on your own and do not eat anything you cannot identify with total confidence. Wild garlic, rosehips, elderflower, cornel cherries and blackberries are freely picked by everyone.
raw.Landmine awareness — non-negotiable: BHMAC reports more than 820 km² of Bosnia still suspected of contamination, roughly 1.6% of the country, from an original 4,180 km²; clearance is running at about 75 km² per year and the country is not expected to be mine-free before the early 2030s. The former front line ran through this region. Stay on marked paths, roads, and land that is obviously farmed or grazed. Do not walk into unused meadow, ruined villages, or forest edge to photograph a building. Yellow-and-red skull signs and red-painted stones mean stop. Report anything suspicious rather than moving it.
raw.Wildlife: Brown bear and grey wolf both use the Osječenica–Klekovača massif; otter is genuinely common on the Una and the Unac and is the realistic sighting — look at dawn from the Martin Brod bridges and the quiet reaches above Lohovo. Kingfisher, dipper and grey heron work the travertine steps all day. Ethical viewing: no baiting, no drones over roosts or otter holts, keep to hides and bridges, and give any bear a wide, upwind exit.
raw.Fire risk and open flame: Federation forest law bans open fire in and within 150 m of forest during the declared high-risk summer period, typically 1 June–31 October, with cantonal variations. Use only the built fire pits at cabins and campsites, never leave one unattended, and expect campfires to be flatly refused inside national park zones.

sources.confidenceNotes: The park price list checked was the most recent published version and may not reflect a 2026 revision — re-verify before publishing. Named accommodation other than the park's own Camp Lučica needs confirmation of current operation, rates and season; the rafting-operator bungalow cluster is described generically for that reason and should have a specific verified operator inserted. Rafting per-person prices are operator-set and were not confirmed this run. The Klekovača/Osječenica forest-road condition, logging activity and which tracks are cleared ground must be confirmed locally on the day — treat every figure about them as indicative. EU–Western Balkans roaming rates changed in 2023 and are being revised again; check current caps. Una Regatta dates shift annually. Cross-border rental fees from Croatia vary by company.
